title: Why the Samaritan discourse spans two books; ask and you receive
english: Perhaps, Ambrose — most God-loving and most devout — you would have preferred that the discourse on the Samaritan woman not be broken, so that part of it stood in the twelfth book and the sequel in the thirteenth. But when we saw that the twelfth book of the commentary had already taken a sufficient compass, we judged it right to end at her words about the well — how Jacob gave it, and drank from it himself, with his sons and his flocks — and to open the thirteenth from our Lord’s reply to her.

[[Jesus answered and said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up to eternal life.” >> Bible:John 4:13-14]] (In our lemma the clause “will never thirst forever, but the water that I will give him” has dropped out; Preuschen marks the gap.)

This is Jesus’ second answer to the Samaritan woman. First he had said, [[“If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” >> Bible:John 4:10]] Now, as if coaxing her to ask for that living water, he speaks the words before us. To the first speech she gave no assent; she only raised a difficulty about comparing the two waters. After the Lord’s second answer she receives what was said and replies, [[“Give me this water.” >> Bible:John 4:15]]

Perhaps it is a standing rule that no one receives a divine gift who does not ask for it. Even the Father, through the psalm, urges the Savior himself to ask so that the gift may be granted him — as the Son teaches us: [[“The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.’” >> Bible:Psalm 2:7-8]] And the Savior says, [[“Ask, and it will be given you”; “for everyone who asks receives.” >> Bible:Matthew 7:7-8]]

So the Samaritan woman is persuaded to ask Jesus for water. As we said before, she is a figure of the heterodox who busy themselves with the divine Scriptures: once she hears the comparison of the two waters, look how she had been drinking from a well she thought deep, yet found no rest and was not rid of thirst.

title: Two senses of thirst and hunger: emptiness-need and chronic want
english: Let us see what is meant by [[“Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again.” >> Bible:John 4:13]] In bodily speech, “to thirst” and “to hunger” each carry two senses. One is the need we feel when emptied and drawn toward food or drink because moisture has run short. The other is the way the poor, short of necessities, keep saying they hunger or thirst even when they have just taken something.

The first sense is plain in Exodus: when they lacked food they murmured; when they lacked water and thirsted they murmured against Moses, [[“What shall we drink?” >> Bible:Exodus 15:24]] And at Rephidim [[the people thirsted for water and murmured against Moses. >> Bible:Exodus 17:1-3]]

The second sense has a clear parallel in Paul: [[“To the present hour we hunger and thirst and are poorly clothed.” >> Bible:1 Corinthians 4:11]] The first sort of hunger and thirst necessarily visits healthy bodies; the second visits those already worn down by want.

title: Which thirst Jesus means; deep words that leave the same aporia
english: We must also ask, in [[“Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,” >> Bible:John 4:13]] which thirst is meant. Taken bodily, the point is likely this: even if a drink fills you for the moment, as soon as it settles the same feeling returns — you thirst again, back where you began.
He adds, [[“Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will have in him a spring of water leaping up to eternal life.” >> Bible:John 4:14]] Who can still thirst while a spring is within him?

But the leading sense is this: the person who takes a share in deep words may rest for a little, accepting the deepest thoughts he draws up and thinks he has found; yet when he looks again he will raise fresh difficulties about the very points on which he rested, because the “depth” he supposed cannot give a clear, sharp grasp of what he seeks.

So even if someone is swept along and assents to the persuasiveness of what is said, later he finds in himself the same perplexity he had before he learned these things. My word, by contrast, is such that the spring of the life-giving drink arises in the one who receives what I announce; and the one who takes my water is helped so far that a spring welling up within him finds out everything sought.

title: The spring within fulfills hunger and thirst for righteousness
english: The one who drinks the water Jesus will give will have within him that [[spring of water leaping up to eternal life >> Bible:John 4:14]] when the promise spoken over those who hunger and thirst for righteousness is filled out. For the Word says, [[“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” >> Bible:Matthew 5:6]]

And perhaps, because one must hunger and thirst for righteousness before being filled, we have to let hunger and thirst be formed in us if we are to be satisfied — so that we may say, [[“As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.” >> Bible:Psalm 42:1]]

title: Scripture’s well versus the leap of the water Jesus gives
english: We should also ask whether another kind of help — the help of those who have kept company with the truth itself — can be set apart from the help we think we get from the Scriptures even when they are read accurately. The sign is this: whoever drinks from Jacob’s spring thirsts again; whoever drinks the water Jesus gives has within him [[a spring of water leaping up to eternal life. >> Bible:John 4:14]]

Those who handle the Scriptures carefully and gather sound teaching from them drink from Jacob’s spring, as Jacob himself did, with his sons and his flocks. Those who twist the Scriptures and prop up ugly doctrines under the pretext of having understood them drink as the Samaritan woman drank before she believed in Jesus.

title: Things beyond what is written; thunder-words and unspeakable words
english: If we say there are things beyond what is written, we do not mean that the many can know them. We mean what John heard and was not allowed to write — [[the words of the thunders >> Bible:Revelation 10:4]] — learning them yet sparing the world by not writing them, because he judged that [[the world itself could not contain the books that would be written. >> Bible:John 21:25]]

So too with what Paul learned: [[unspeakable words >> Bible:2 Corinthians 12:4]] beyond what is written — if humans have in fact spoken what stands written. [[What eye has not seen >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:9]] is beyond the written; what ear has not heard cannot be written down. And what has never risen upon a human heart is greater than Jacob’s spring: it is shown from [[the spring of water leaping up to eternal life >> Bible:John 4:14]] to those who no longer have only a human heart, but can say, [[“We have the mind of Christ.” >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:16]]

title: “Give me this water”: she names him Lord a second time and receives
english: [[The woman says to him, “Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst or keep coming here to draw.” >> Bible:John 4:15]] This is already the second time the Samaritan woman names the Savior “Lord.” First it was, [[“Lord, you have no bucket, and the well is deep” >> Bible:John 4:11]] — when she also longed to know where he got living water, and whether he was greater than Jacob, whom she counted her father. Now she asks for the water that becomes, in the one who drinks, [[a spring leaping up to eternal life. >> Bible:John 4:14]]

And if it is true that [[“If you asked him, he would have given you living water,” >> Bible:John 4:10]] then when she said, “Give me this water,” she received living water — so that she need no longer be at a loss in thirst, or keep going to Jacob’s spring to draw, but may behold the truth in an angelic way, beyond the human, even without Jacob’s water. For angels do not need Jacob’s spring in order to drink; each has within himself a spring of water leaping up to eternal life.

title: “Go call your husband”: the rebuke that opens her confession
english: [[Jesus says to her, “Go, call your husband and come here.” >> Bible:John 4:16]] [[The woman answered, “I have no husband.” >> Bible:John 4:17]] [[Jesus says to her, “You have said well, ‘I have no husband’; for you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband; this you have said truly.” >> Bible:John 4:17-18]]
Through this, it seems to me, the Savior convicts her as caught in adultery, so that once she comes to awareness of her sins she may ask for release and receive cleansing from the living water.

title: Five husbands as the senses; a sixth, unsound “spiritual” partner
english: I take it that every soul being led into devotion to God in Christ through the Scriptures begins from what is said about sense and body, and so has five husbands — one answering to each of the senses.

But when, after keeping company with sense-things, someone wants to lift up his head and is urged toward the intelligibles, yet meets a word that is not sound though it claims a “spiritual” allegory, that person leaves the five and takes another — giving, so to speak, a bill of divorce to the first five and choosing to live with a sixth.

And until Jesus comes and brings us to awareness of that kind of husband, we stay with him. When the Lord has come and spoken with us, we deny that husband and say, [[“I have no husband.” >> Bible:John 4:17]]

title: Heracleon on Jacob’s water as weak, temporary, worldly
english: Let us also look at Heracleon on the passage. He says that that life, and the opinion that went with it, had become weak, temporary, and failing; for it was worldly, he claims, and he thinks he proves its worldliness from the fact that Jacob’s flocks drank from it.

If by “weak, temporary, and failing” he meant knowledge in part — either knowledge from the Scriptures set beside [[the unspeakable words a human may not utter, >> Bible:2 Corinthians 12:4]] or all the knowledge that now comes [[through a mirror and in a riddle, >> Bible:1 Corinthians 13:12]] to be abolished when the perfect comes — we would not charge him. But if he says this to slander the ancient Scriptures, he is to be blamed.

He is not wrong when he says the water the Savior gives is from his Spirit and power. He goes astray, though, when he takes [[“will never thirst forever” >> Bible:John 4:14]] as a lesson pointing only to life supplied from above, and cites as proof [[“Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst or keep coming here to draw,” >> Bible:John 4:15]] as though the Samaritan woman had understood the saying in a merely bodily way and had simply voiced her own feeling.

title: Heracleon on “Go call your husband”: pleroma consort forced onto the text
english: Heracleon also takes [[“He says to her” >> Bible:John 4:16]] this way: Jesus means, in effect, “If you want this water, go call your husband.” Heracleon thinks the “husband” the Savior names is the Samaritan woman’s pleroma, so that once she comes with that consort to the Savior she may receive power, union, and blending with the pleroma.

As for a worldly husband, Heracleon says, Jesus told her to call one because he knew the man she had was not her lawful husband. But that reading plainly forces the text. If [[“Call your husband and come here” >> Bible:John 4:16]] meant the consort from the pleroma, Jesus would also have had to say how she was to call him so that she might come with him to the Savior.

Heracleon himself says that in the deeper sense she did not know her own husband, while in the plain sense she was ashamed to admit she had an adulterer rather than a husband. How, then, is it not empty for the Savior to tell her, “Call your husband”?

title: Third “Lord”; “I see you are a prophet”; five husbands versus Heracleon’s six
english: [[The woman says to him, “Lord, I see that you are a prophet.” >> Bible:John 4:19]] This is already the third time the Samaritan woman names the Savior “Lord”: first, [[“Lord, you have no bucket” >> Bible:John 4:11]]; again, [[“Lord, give me this water” >> Bible:John 4:15]]; and now when she also calls him a prophet.
We read, [[“You have had five husbands.” >> Bible:John 4:18]] Beside Heracleon we found, “You have had six husbands,” and he takes the six to mean the whole of material evil.

She does not yet think him greater than the prophets, nor the one the prophets foretold, but only a prophet. So too the heterodox mind: once her five earlier husbands and the later seeming-husband have been exposed, she calls the Word that exposed them a prophet — someone divine, better than a mere human.

title: Gerizim and Zion: Samaritans as figure of the heterodox
english: Even now, if Samaritans and Jews enter debate, each will press the other. The Samaritan will use this woman’s words: [[“Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” >> Bible:John 4:20]] — pointing to Gerizim — [[“but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where one must worship.” >> Bible:John 4:20]]

Jews — for [[salvation is from them >> Bible:John 4:22]] — figure those who hold sound teaching; Samaritans figure the heterodox. So they treat Gerizim as divine. The name means Cutting-apart or Division, matching the historical split of the ten tribes from the two in Jeroboam’s days — and Jeroboam’s own name means Splitting of a people. Jews, by contrast, hold to Zion, which means Watchtower.

title: Two “hours are coming”: perfection beyond bodies, and progress already now
english: [[“An hour is coming” >> Bible:John 4:21]] is written twice. The first time [[“and now is” >> Bible:John 4:23]] is not added; the second time it is. I take the first to mark worship beyond bodies that will stand in at perfection; the second to mark the progress of those being perfected in this life as far as human nature allows.

So one may already worship the Father in spirit and truth when the hour is not only coming but also now is. When Scripture says, [[“An hour is coming, and now is,” >> Bible:John 4:23]] it no longer adds, [[“neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem,” >> Bible:John 4:21]] — the clause that stands where “an hour is coming” is written without “now is.”

title: Heracleon on the prophet and the woman’s question about worship
english: On the same words Heracleon says the Samaritan woman has fittingly confessed what Jesus said. A prophet, he claims, is only one who knows all things — which not everyone knows — and yet “the prophet does not know all things.”

By [[“Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” >> Bible:John 4:20]] he wants the pre-law worship of the nations; by [[“You say that in Jerusalem” >> Bible:John 4:20]] the Jews’ worship under the law. He casts the Samaritan woman as having left the city of God’s will through ignorance and neglect, and so fallen into fornication.
These claims are easy to overturn. Where has he shown that only the all-knowing one is a prophet, or that a prophet does not know all things?

title: Heracleon on “Believe me, woman”: creation as desert of beasts
english: Heracleon thought he had spotted something clever: earlier Jesus had not said, [[“Believe me, woman,” >> Bible:John 4:21]] but now he commands it. That observation muddies his own case.

He says creation is a desert haunt of beasts, which all worshiped before the law; Jerusalem stands for the creator, whom the Jews worshiped. “You,” he says, “will worship neither creation nor the demiurge, but the Father of truth.” He even counts the woman already among the true worshipers.
But if angels do not worship the Father in Jerusalem, how can those greater than Jerusalem’s worshipers fail to worship the Father?

title: “You worship what you do not know”: heterodox guesswork versus Jewish revelation
english: [[“You” >> Bible:John 4:22]], on the surface, means Samaritans; by ascent, those who hold heterodox views of the Scriptures. [[“We” >> Bible:John 4:22]], on the surface, means Jews; by allegory, I the Word and those shaped after me, who have salvation from the Jewish oracles.
What the heterodox worship is invention, not truth — myth, not mystery. The one who worships the Creator, especially as the Jew in secret and by the prophets’ spiritual words, knows what he worships.
I cannot see how, when the Savior says outright that [[“salvation is from the Jews,” >> Bible:John 4:22]] the heterodox still deny the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

title: True worshipers walk in the Spirit; not every claim to worship counts
english: Those who do not even claim to worship the Father should not be called worshipers of God at all. Among all who do claim to worship the Creator, some are no longer in the flesh but in the Spirit — they walk by the Spirit and do not carry out the flesh’s desire — while others are not in the Spirit but in the flesh and wage war according to the flesh. Then we must call true worshipers those who worship in the Spirit, and not true those who remain in the flesh.

[[“But an hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.” >> Bible:John 4:23]] I still cannot see how the heterodox deny Abraham’s God when the Savior says salvation is from the Jews.

title: Heracleon on “We worship”: aeon-companions and salvation from Judea
english: Heracleon takes [[“We worship” >> Bible:John 4:22]] to mean those in an aeon and those who came with him: they, he says, knew whom they worshiped, and worshiped in truth.

On [[“salvation is from the Jews,” >> Bible:John 4:22]] he says Christ was born in Judea, and from that nation salvation and the Word went out into the world. In the deeper sense he tells the story as if the Jews were images of those in the pleroma.
He ought, then, to show for each act of worship how it images what is in the pleroma — if they mean this not only in words but in truth.

title: The Father seeks true worshipers; Heracleon’s “lost in deep matter” myth
english: [[For the Father seeks such as these to worship him. >> Bible:John 4:23]] If the Father seeks, he seeks through the Son who came [[to seek and save the lost >> Bible:Luke 19:10]] — cleansing them and training them by the Word and by sound teaching until he makes them true worshipers.

Heracleon says what belongs to the Father has been lost in the deep matter of error, and is sought so that the Father may be worshiped by his own. If he meant the story of the lost sheep or of the Father’s son who fell away, we might have accepted the telling.
But his school spins myths and never states clearly what this lost spiritual nature is, or what times or ages preceded its loss. So we gladly leave them aside.

title: “God is spirit”: not a bodily substance but the giver of true life
english: Many have said many things about God and his substance — some that he is a fine bodily and ethereal nature, others that he is incorporeal and of a substance beyond these. We should ask whether the divine Scriptures give us any start for speaking of God’s substance.

Here it is said, in a manner of speaking, that spirit is his substance. The apostle says, [[“And the Lord is the Spirit.” >> Bible:2 Corinthians 3:17]] John says, [[“God is light.” >> Bible:1 John 1:5]] The law says, [[“Our God is a consuming fire.” >> Bible:Hebrews 12:29]]

So I take [[“God is spirit” >> Bible:John 4:24]] this way: just as we are kept alive in ordinary life by the breath around us, God is called spirit because he leads us into true life. [[For the Spirit gives life. >> Bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]]

title: Bodily names for God are figurative, as with eyes and hands
english: First: when Scripture gives God eyes, ears, hands, and feet, we read those words figuratively and refuse those who wrap a human shape around God. We should treat the other names the same way.

That is already clear from what is plain: [[“God is light,” >> Bible:1 John 1:5]] says John, [[“and in him is no darkness at all.” >> Bible:1 John 1:5]] How can one take him as light except tropically?

title: God as light lights the mind, not the body’s sun-work
english: That settled, what should we think of God called light, in whom is no darkness? Does he light bodily eyes, or the mind’s eyes of which the prophet says, [[“Lighten my eyes, lest I sleep in death”? >> Bible:Psalm 13:3]]

It is obvious we should not make God do the sun’s job while leaving another to light the eyes of those who will not sleep unto death. God lights the mind of those he judges worthy of his own illumination.

title: Spirit given and withdrawn: dust without it, renewal with it

title: Heracleon on “God is spirit”: unclean claim that worshipers are homoousios
english: On [[“God is spirit” >> Bible:John 4:24]] Heracleon says God’s divine nature is undefiled, pure, and invisible. I do not see how that explains how God is spirit.

Worse: he calls those who worship in spirit homoousios with the unbegotten and all-blessed nature. That is impious. Only a little earlier Heracleon himself said they had fallen — that the Samaritan woman, though of a spiritual nature, had gone out into fornication.
They do not see that what is homoousios is also capable of the same things. If she fornicated, she was no longer homoousios with God.

title: The Samaritan woman expects Christ from the Mosaic books alone

They likely draw that hope from Jacob’s blessing on Judah: [[“A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things stored up for him come.” >> Bible:Genesis 49:10]]

title: She leaves the water-jar: zeal for the city’s good over the bodily errand
english: [[So the woman left her water-jar and went away into the city and says to the people, “Come, see a human who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?” >> Bible:John 4:28-29]]

title: A woman evangelizes Christ first here; later a woman announces the resurrection
english: Here a woman announces the Christ; at the end of the Gospels a woman who saw him before all the others tells the apostles of the Savior’s resurrection.
Those from the city went out and were coming to him — going out, as it were, to do good. Such readings ask for a careful ascent into what is written about the water-jar.
